title: Volleyball
description: Volleyball in Signature form is a game of three touches and one net: receive, lift, and strike, with six players moving as a single unit. The rotation rule is the game's quiet teacher, because it forces every player to serve, defend, and attack rather than hiding in a single role. A rally ends when the ball lands, is blocked back, or is mishandled, and the two-point margin keeps sets honest to the end instead of letting a single lucky point decide them. The libero, a defensive specialist in a different shirt, shows how a team game can honour a specialist without breaking its rotation. Played well, volleyball looks like a conversation: the pass asks a question, the set shapes it, and the spike answers it.

history: Volleyball was invented in 1895 in Massachusetts as a gentler indoor game, and it grew into an Olympic sport with indoor and beach forms.
rules: Two teams of six hit a ball over a net, scoring when the ball lands on the opponent's court or the opponents fail to return it, with sets played to 25 points.
techniques: Key skills are the serve, pass, set, spike, and block, combined in a three-touch pattern: pass, set, attack.

title: Handball
description: Signature handball is speed made into a team game: seven against seven, a small ball, and a goal that rewards the thrower who finds a gap. The three-second, three-step rule is what keeps it fast, because no player can stall with the ball and wait for a perfect opening; the team must move, pass, and shoot in rhythm. Defenders form a wall of six, goalkeepers read shots from nine metres and closer, and fast breaks punish any team that celebrates a goal too long. Goals come often, which means a lead is never safe and a comeback is always plausible, and that is why handball crowds stay loud to the final whistle.

history: Modern team handball developed in northern Europe in the early twentieth century and became an Olympic sport in 1972 for men and 1976 for women.
rules: Two teams of seven play on an indoor court, passing and throwing a ball into the opponent's goal, with matches of two 30-minute halves.
techniques: Players use jump shots, fast breaks, and set plays against a six-player defence, with a goalkeeper guarding a goal three metres wide.

title: Netball
description: Signature netball is a passing game built on zones: seven positions, three thirds, and a ring without a backboard, so every goal must be earned by movement and accuracy. The no-dribbling rule changes everything, because a player who receives the ball must decide and deliver within three seconds, and the footwork rule means that decision must be made on a planted foot. Zones stop any one star from doing everything: the centre links the thirds, the shooters finish, and the defenders protect the circle. It is a game that rewards teams over individuals, since a single brilliant player cannot carry the ball the length of the court alone.

history: Netball grew from early women's basketball in the 1890s, with its own rules formalised in England, and it is now played widely across the Commonwealth.
rules: Two teams of seven play on a court divided into thirds, with restricted positions, no dribbling, and shooting only from the goal circle.
techniques: Passing, footwork, and positional play dominate, since players may hold the ball for three seconds and must stay within their assigned zones.

title: Korfball
description: Signature korfball is the mixed game by design: four men and four women per side, a basket on a pole with no backboard, and marking matched by gender. The ban on running with the ball and on contact makes it a pure passing and shooting contest, where space is created by movement rather than by pushing past a defender. Zone swaps after every two goals keep every player honest, because attackers must also defend and defenders must also attack. The height of the basket, three and a half metres, rewards a clean, high-arcing shot over a defender's reach. It is a sport whose fairness is written into its structure, not added afterwards.

history: Korfball was invented in the Netherlands in 1902 by Nico Broekhuysen as a mixed-gender sport, and it remains the best-known mixed team ball sport.
rules: Two mixed teams of eight, four men and four women, score by throwing a ball through a basket on a pole, with no running with the ball and no physical contact.
techniques: Players shoot from distance, use passing and movement to create space, and swap attack and defence zones after every two goals.

title: Dodgeball
description: Signature dodgeball turns a playground game into a contest of nerve: throw to eliminate, dodge to survive, and catch to turn the match around. The catch rule is the heart of the game, because a single good catch both removes the thrower and brings a teammate back, swinging the numbers in one moment. Blocking with a held ball gives a defender a shield, but a dropped block costs the player, so every defensive choice carries risk. Timed games mean a team that is behind on numbers can still win by surviving, and a team that is ahead must press without throwing wildly. It is fast, loud, and forgiving to beginners, since a new player can contribute by dodging and retrieving balls from the first minute.

history: Dodgeball grew from playground games into organised leagues with written rules, national associations, and world championships.
rules: Two teams throw balls at opponents to eliminate them, while dodging, catching, and blocking; a caught ball eliminates the thrower and revives a teammate in many rule sets.
techniques: Throwing accuracy, dodging, catching, and court awareness matter most, with teamwork in targeting and ball retrieval.

title: Ultimate Frisbee
description: Signature ultimate is a passing game played with a disc instead of a ball, and its most distinctive rule is that there is no referee: players call their own fouls and settle them by talking. That self-officiating only works because the sport's culture, Spirit of the Game, treats honesty as part of winning rather than as an obstacle to it. On the field, the game is about cutting: a thrower with a disc they cannot carry must rely on teammates moving into space, and a good cut creates a throwing lane where none existed a second before. Layout catches, diving to intercept a disc, give the sport its spectacle, but its soul is the pass, the cut, and the conversation after a contested call.

history: Ultimate was invented by students in New Jersey in 1968 and grew into a worldwide sport governed by the World Flying Disc Federation.
rules: Two teams of seven pass a flying disc up the field to score in an end zone, with no running with the disc and self-officiating under the Spirit of the Game.
techniques: Throwing forehands and backhands, cutting to get open, and zone or man defence shape play, with layout catches for spectacular defensive plays.

title: Softball
description: Signature softball is baseball's close cousin with its own character: a bigger ball, an underarm pitch, seven innings, and a field small enough that every play feels close. Fastpitch pitching is the game's engine, with rise and drop balls that move late and change-ups that break a batter's timing, all delivered from a flat circle rather than a mound. Slap hitting, where a batter moves toward first base while making contact, turns speed into a weapon and rewards left-handed batters who can place the ball. The smaller field compresses decisions: outfielders throw sooner, infielders react faster, and a single base-running mistake can end an inning.

history: Softball began in Chicago in 1887 as an indoor version of baseball and became an Olympic sport, with fastpitch the elite form.
rules: Two teams of nine or ten play seven innings, with underarm pitching from a flat circle, a larger ball, and a smaller field than baseball.
techniques: Hitting, slap hitting, base running, and pitching with rise, drop, and change-up pitches define the game.

title: Baseball
description: Signature baseball is a game of duels inside a team contest: pitcher against batter, runner against fielder, manager against manager. Nine innings give the contest room to breathe, with three outs per half-inning and extra innings when scores are level, so a team that trails early has time to recover. The pitcher's arsenal, fastball, curve, slider, change-up, is a study in deception, because a batter must decide in a fraction of a second whether and where to swing. Fielders read batters and shift, managers time substitutions, and base runners gamble on extra bases. It is a slow game only to those who miss its strategy; to its players, every pitch is a decision.

history: Baseball developed in the United States in the nineteenth century from earlier bat-and-ball games, with the Knickerbocker rules of 1845 an early codification.
rules: Two teams of nine play nine innings, with pitchers throwing overarm, batters hitting, and runs scored by circling four bases.
techniques: Pitching, hitting, fielding, and base running are the core skills, with strategy in pitch selection, defensive shifts, and substitutions.

title: Field Hockey
description: Signature field hockey is speed on turf with a stick that has only one legal face: the flat side, which forces players to shape every touch with a single surface. The shooting circle is the game's boundary of meaning, because a goal only counts from inside it, so attacks must penetrate rather than merely shoot from distance. Penalty corners turn a defensive foul into a set-piece battle, with a drag flicker striking a ball pushed out from the back line at high speed while defenders rush from the goal. Goalkeepers, armoured in helmet and pads, are the last line in a game where the ball moves faster than most players can run.

history: Modern field hockey was codified in England in the nineteenth century and became an Olympic sport in 1908 for men and 1980 for women.
rules: Two teams of eleven play on turf with curved sticks, scoring by hitting the ball into the opponent's goal, in four quarters of 15 minutes.
techniques: Dribbling, passing, tackling with the flat side of the stick, drag flicks at penalty corners, and goalkeeping in full protective gear define play.

title: Ice Hockey
description: Signature ice hockey is the fastest team game on skates: six on the ice, a puck instead of a ball, and shifts so short that fresh legs are a tactic. Rolling substitutions mean a coach manages energy as carefully as tactics, sending lines out for bursts and resting them before fatigue costs a goal. The puck's speed and the rink's boards create a game of rebounds and deflections, where a shot that misses can come straight back into play. Goaltenders, padded and masked, face shots from close range and decide matches with saves that look impossible until they are made. It is a sport where skating skill is not an extra but the entry ticket.

history: Ice hockey developed in Canada in the nineteenth century from stick games on ice and became a major professional and Olympic sport.
rules: Two teams of six on the ice, including a goaltender, skate and pass a puck, scoring in the opponent's goal, in three 20-minute periods.
techniques: Skating, stickhandling, passing, shooting, body checking, and goaltending combine at high speed on a rink.

title: Water Polo
description: Signature water polo is a team game played without a floor: seven per side in deep water, treading with the eggbeater kick, passing and shooting while wrestling for position. The eggbeater kick is the sport's hidden skill, because a player who cannot stay upright and free their hands cannot pass, shoot, or defend at all. The shot clock keeps attacks honest, exclusions punish major fouls with a 20-second disadvantage, and the goalkeeper alone may use two hands. It is exhausting by design, and that exhaustion is part of its fairness: the fittest team can hold its shape in the fourth quarter, when a tired team falls apart.

history: Water polo developed in Britain in the nineteenth century as a water version of rugby and football, and became an Olympic sport in 1900.
rules: Two teams of seven in the water, including a goalkeeper, pass and shoot a ball into the opponent's goal, in four quarters of eight minutes.
techniques: Swimming, treading water, passing, shooting, and wrestling for position combine, with players using an eggbeater kick to stay upright.

title: Lacrosse
description: Signature lacrosse carries the oldest roots in this pair: a stickball tradition of Indigenous North America, codified in Canada and now played worldwide. The pocket is the game's instrument, because a player must cradle the ball while sprinting and dodging, keeping it in the net through contact and change of direction. Field lacrosse fields ten per side, with face-offs restarting play and fast breaks rewarding teams that move the ball before a defence sets. It blends three familiar games at once: hockey's speed, basketball's passing, and soccer's field strategy, yet it feels like none of them, because the stick changes every skill it touches.

history: Lacrosse descends from stickball games played by Indigenous peoples of North America and was codified in Canada in the nineteenth century.
rules: Two teams use sticks with a netted pocket to carry, pass, and shoot a ball into the opponent's goal, in four quarters.
techniques: Cradling, passing, dodging, shooting, and checking combine speed, hand-eye coordination, and teamwork.

title: Rugby League
description: Signature rugby league is rugby stripped to its contest of tackles: thirteen per side, six tackles to make progress, and then the ball changes hands. The six-tackle rule is the game's metronome, because it forces an attacking team to plan its last tackle, often a kick, before the count runs out. Play-the-balls restart play quickly, so the game rarely stalls, and the scoring values, four for a try, two for a goal, one for a drop goal, keep comebacks within reach. It is a hard, direct game, built on running lines, tackling technique, and the discipline to use six tackles wisely rather than wastefully.

history: Rugby league split from rugby union in England in 1895 over payments to players, and developed its own rules and professional leagues.
rules: Two teams of thirteen play two 40-minute halves, with six tackles to advance before handing over possession, and tries worth four points.
techniques: Running, passing, tackling, kicking, and set plays from scrums and play-the-balls shape the game.

title: Rugby Union
description: Signature rugby union is the fifteen-a-side contest for the ball itself: scrums, lineouts, rucks, and mauls all decide who keeps possession, and possession decides who can score. A try is worth five, a conversion two, and penalty and drop goals three each, so a team can build a lead in several ways and a trailing team can chase it in several ways. The set piece is the game's signature: a scrum tests a pack's strength and timing, a lineout tests jumping and lifting, and a maul tests a team's ability to drive together. It is a game of phases, where patience and territory matter as much as a single break, and where every position, from prop to fullback, has a distinct job.

history: Rugby union was codified in England in 1871, grew into a worldwide amateur and then professional sport, and holds a World Cup every four years.
rules: Two teams of fifteen play two 40-minute halves, with tries worth five points, scrums, lineouts, rucks, and mauls contesting possession.
techniques: Running, passing, kicking, tackling, scrummaging, lineout jumping, and tactical kicking combine in a game of continuous contest for the ball.

title: Sepak Takraw
description: Signature sepak takraw is volleyball played without hands: three per side, a net, and a rattan ball struck with feet, head, knees, and chest. The bicycle kick spike is its defining image, a player airborne, twisting, and striking the ball over the net with a foot, but the sport's real skill is quieter: the first touch that sets up the second, and the second that places the third for a spike. Three touches, like volleyball, give the game its rhythm, and the ban on hands forces a kind of athleticism most team sports never demand. It is a Southeast Asian game with a worldwide following, and it rewards flexibility and timing above brute force.

history: Sepak takraw descends from kick volleyball games in Southeast Asia and is now an international sport with Asian Games and world championships.
rules: Two teams of three play on a badminton-sized court over a net, striking a rattan or synthetic ball with feet, head, knees, and chest, but not hands.
techniques: Acrobatic bicycle kicks, blocks at the net, and precise serves define the sport, which demands flexibility, timing, and aerial skill.

title: Bandy
description: Signature bandy is soccer on skates: eleven per side, a field the size of a soccer pitch, and a ball instead of a puck, played in two halves of forty-five minutes. The soccer resemblance is deliberate, with offside, corners, and free strokes adapted to ice, but the skating changes everything, because players cover ground faster and the ball runs further on a frozen surface. Goals come often, since a large field and a fast ball punish any defence that loses its shape. It is a winter sport with a loyal northern heartland, and its endurance demand is plain: ninety minutes of skating, passing, and shooting, with no boards to lean on and no bench to hide on for long.

history: Bandy developed in England in the nineteenth century as hockey on ice and is now strongest in Russia, Sweden, Finland, and Norway.
rules: Two teams of eleven skate on a large ice field, using curved sticks to hit a ball into the opponent's goal, in two 45-minute halves.
techniques: Skating endurance, long passing, shooting, and goalkeeping on a field the size of a soccer pitch define the game.
